analysis.one_liner: Bars CEOs convicted of financial crimes from serving in executive branch positions.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 3, 2025 with 10 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, the bill was referred to the House Oversight Committee and has had no further action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would disqualify anyone who served as a company's chief executive officer from being appointed to any executive branch job if they were finally convicted of crimes like fraud, bribery, insider trading, embezzlement, tax evasion, or wage theft. A person found serving in violation would be removed. It was introduced by Rep. Chris Deluzio, a Pennsylvania Democrat, and sent to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want government appointments filled by people without fraud or corruption convictions. The bill applies to future appointments across the executive branch, from cabinet agencies to regulatory posts, where industry executives often move between corporate boardrooms and the agencies that oversee them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone wary of convicted executives in government

how_it_helps.text: Anyone who served as a CEO and was finally convicted of a covered crime — bribery, corruption, embezzlement, fraud, insider trading, wage theft, tax evasion, cybercrime, or copyright infringement — is ineligible for appointment to an executive branch position [S2].
Anyone found serving in violation of the restriction must be removed from their executive branch post [S2].
Wage theft and insider trading are explicitly named as covered crimes, directly targeting misconduct that harms workers and markets rather than only classic government bribery [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Corporate executives with criminal convictions for financial crimes lose access to a career path that has historically run from the C-suite into government. Presidents and agency heads lose some flexibility in choosing appointees. The bill applies to covered crimes regardless of whether the conviction was a felony or misdemeanor.
analysis.who_pays_short: Convicted corporate executives seeking government jobs

drawbacks.text: The covered-crime list is broad and includes vague categories like 'corruption,' 'cybercrime,' and 'copyright infringement,' and the bill does not distinguish between serious felonies and minor offenses, so a relatively small conviction could trigger a lifetime ban from government service [S2].
The ban applies only to chief executive officers, not other senior executives — CFOs, general counsels, or board members with the same kind of convictions would remain eligible [S2].
The restriction reaches only appointed positions in the executive branch; it does nothing about corporate executives serving in Congress or staying in the private sector [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — keeping people convicted of defrauding investors, workers, or the government out of the agencies meant to police those very abuses — is a modest but genuine integrity safeguard, especially given the frequency of executive-to-regulator career moves. Its weaknesses are design ones: the crime categories are loosely defined and could catch minor offenses, while the CEO-only focus leaves large gaps. The bill is narrow enough that its real-world effect would be limited either way.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee on June 3, 2025, and nothing has happened to it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Deluzio introduced the bill on June 3, 2025, joined by original cosponsors including Reps. Neguse, Ryan, Sykes, Craig, and Scholten [S2].
The House referred it to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform the same day, and the action history shows no further steps — no committee vote or floor action has occurred [S4].
The bill has 10 cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: corporate executives with convictions for fraud, bribery, or wage theft remain fully eligible for executive branch appointments, and no committee action has been taken to change that.

industries.industry: Corporate executives (CEOs of companies with government career ambitions)
industries.note: Executives convicted of fraud, bribery, insider trading, wage theft, tax evasion, or related crimes would lose eligibility for executive branch appointments — the very posts where industry insiders often shape the rules for their former industries. Keeping that revolving door closed serves the public's interest in impartial enforcement.

analysis.trajectory: Bills that sit in committee without a hearing or markup, with no cosponsors from the majority party, rarely reach the floor. Unless the bill picks up Republican support or the committee schedules action, it will most likely die at the end of this Congress without a vote.
